24000: Micro-PIXE (proton induced X-ray emission) analysis was used to determine the content of strontium in the core area of otoliths from Dolly Varden and Arctic char from the north slope of the Yukon Territory. Otoliths are composed primarily of calcium carbonate (as aragonite). Trace elements such as strontium which are present in the water the fish inhabits and which are chemically similar to calcium are often incorporated into the otoliths. Because otoliths do not undergo resorption of constituents, they contain a permanent record of the environments occupied by the fish throughout life. The otolith core is formed at the site where the individual was spawned; thus, environmental variation in the levels of strontium and other trace elements has the potential to differentiate biological groups of fish. Mean strontium levels in otolith cores from populations of Ivvavik char ranged from 280 to 520 ppm and were associated with the habitat occupied. Strontium differences in otoliths have the potential to discriminate biological stocks of chars in Ivvavik National Park and may also be useful in identifying fish from mixed groups to their stock of origin. This work confirms biological stock structuring observed in these char through other methods.

24001: Since 1984, the National Undersea Research Center at the University of North Carolina at Wilmington has supported over 50 research projects involving the use of shallow and deep submersibles. On every mission numerous hours of videotape were recorded and stored in the Center's archive - often lying dormant after the principal investigators proprietary use period had elapsed. In early 1998, we initiated a project to review each tape and capture representative clips of all fishes, invertebrates and habitat types encountered. Through collaboration with taxonomists, we hope identify all species and make a CD that can be used by the science community.

24002: Seasonality in resource availability and physiological maintenance costs may change the relationships of tradeoffs that balance to maximize fitness. We explore the ways in which recently acquired (income) and stored (capital) energy may be used in reproductive strategies in a seasonally fluctuating environment. We have developed an individual-based model to contrast the fitness of females (measured as lifetime production of offspring) using income and capital modes of reproduction in a seasonal environment. Our model is motivated by the reproductive biology of sailfin mollies, a livebearing fish with facultative investment in egg size. Depending on their body size and lipid stores, females produce large eggs that develop without additional nutritional supplementation (lecithotrophy), or smaller eggs yielding embryos whose nutrition is supplemented during development (lecithotrophy and matrotrophy). Lipid stores vary seasonally from an average of 15% of dry weight in females reproducing in the early spring, to a low of 5% of dry weight in summer-reproducing females. We explore the hypothesis that facultative matrotrophy permits a mixed capital and income-fueled reproductive strategy, and yields maximization of fitness in the face of a tradeoff of egg size and offspring number when compared to pure capital or income strategies.

24003: Gambusia affinis and G. holbrooki from localities like Illinois, North Carolina, and New Jersey stop reproducing in late July to mid-August, when there may be up to two months of mild weather remaining in the season. This is more than enough time to produce an additional litter of young. At the same time, females store up to 20% of their dry mass in fat. These fat reserves are partially utilized during the winter, but some remain the following spring and are used for reproduction. Why would a short-lived species forego producing a litter of young in the late summer in favor of storing fat for reproduction the following spring? We hypothesized that the fitness of young produced in the spring is higher than the hypothetical young that could have been produced the previous fall and that this difference is sufficient to compensate for the risk that the female will not survive to produce a litter the following spring. We tested this hypothesis with enclosure experiments in which we evaluated three components of fitness of newborn young as a function of their date of birth. At four times during the summer, we set out 20 offspring from ten different litters in ten different enclosures, then estimated the probability of survival to maturity, age at maturity and fecundity in the first litter. The last outplant date was after the usual end of the reproductive season and represents the hypothetical last litter of the season. We obtained these litters by keeping females in the laboratory with long photoperiods and high water temperatures. Our results, duplicated in two seasons, demonstrate that the earliest born young have a much higher probability of survival to maturity and much more rapid development than those born late in the season. These two factors will enhance fitness sufficiently under most conditions to favor the early cessation of reproduction.

24004: We determined the variability in year class and brood-specific growth and mortality rates of first-year smallmouth bass (Micropterus dolomieu) and assessed the importance of temperature and spawning date to growth and survival. Date of spawning, hatch, first-feeding and metamorphosis were recorded and growth and survival were estimated for broods from a single population over 5 spawning seasons. Growth and developmental rates were positively associated with water temperature within and among years, but much of the variability in growth rate remained unexplained by temperature. Nest survival was high during the embryonic period in all years, despite low water temperatures, but decreased sharply during the larval and early juvenile periods. Brood-specific mortality rates were highly variable and mortality rate distributions were consistently skewed to the right in all years. Brood-specific mortality rates were weakly to moderately related to spawning date and temperature within years. Brood-specific mortality rates differed significantly among years, but were not related to temperature. Cumulative morality also differed among year classes, but was negatively related to temperature. Our results suggest that temperature may influence first-year recruitment in smallmouth bass through its combined effects on development, growth and mortality, while spawning date ultimately determines the length of the first growing season.

24005: The timing and duration of spawning in smallmouth bass populations are closely tied to body size and spring warming rates. A repeatable pattern of large males preceding small males in the timing of reproduction has been observed at a number of sites. The alternating life history hypothesis proposes that the potential gains made by young-of-year as a consequence of this seasonal pattern of spawning are sufficient to predict size of maturity and spawning time of individuals. We present three lines of evidence that together indicate the acquisition of home ranges in the late juvenile stage is a key process in adult recruitment in our study population in Lake Opeongo. DNA fingerprinting demonstrates a restricted spatial distribution of juveniles in their first summer and little or no size advantage associated with the timing of parental spawning. Home range analysis of adults demonstrates significant fidelity to home ranges, areas of concentrated use and a daily movement pattern suggesting spatial memory. Finally, a 60 year record of age-specific abundance and growth demonstrates that density-dependent growth occurs at ages 2-3; a period of time after their initial restricted distribution in their first summer and prior to the adult home range phase. We believe this transition phase is the key to understanding adult recruitment and that spawning phenology may interact with this element of bass ecology rather than a direct connection to adult maturity as proposed in the alternating life history hypothesis.

24006: Correlations between breeding date and the life history or energy stores of individuals might arise owing to two different mechanisms: condition dependence or adaptation-by-time. Condition dependence is the conventional view, and predicts that individual size, condition, or status influence breeding date. This concept has been profitably applied to iteroparous, income breeding species with flexible breeding times. It seems poorly-suited, however, to some semelparous, capital breeding species that have less flexible breeding times. For these species, a more plausible explanation is that heritable maturation schedules allow temporally-isolated population components to adapt to selective regimes specific to their breeding times (adaptation-by-time). The fundamental difference between the two hypotheses is that condition dependence considers breeding date within a season to be a proximate effect of variation in life history traits or energy allocation, whereas adaptation-by-time considers breeding date to be an ultimate cause of such variation. I present evidence for limited gene flow among temporal components of Pacific salmon populations and evidence that they exhibit adaptive variation tailored to selective regimes that vary through the breeding season. Adaptation-by-time appears relevant to temporal trends in body size, reproductive life span, patterns of energy allocation, and the development rate of embryos.

24007: Seasonality leads to time constraints on the major life history transitions. I review recent theory that develops predictions on the patterns of age and size at maturity expected in seasonal environments. Unfortunately common patterns in life history transitions may result from a variety of constraints imposed by or even unrelated to seasonality. Therefore, studies that center primarily upon observation and pattern offer little to disentangling the various forces that can lead to common patterns. Experimental methods are required for this task. I review a series of experiments on a variety of taxa that have informed these issues. I focus on two predictions. First, individuals approaching a time horizon are expected to take greater foraging risks and thereby decrease their time to maturity. Second, independent of any behavioural responses, organisms approaching a time horizon are expected to accelerate development and similarly decrease time to maturity. The experimental results lend support to these hypotheses.

24008: The seasonal timing of reproduction may vary with individual characteristics (or 'state variables'), such as size and energetic state. I review this phenomenon in fishes. I show that the pattern is widespread, in taxonomic terms and across reproductive modes and behaviors. I show that there is evidence that individual state can affect the timing of first reproduction in the season (onset) as well as the last breeding effort of the season (termination), in serially-spawning fishes. The most common observation is that large individuals commence breeding activity earlier in the season than small individuals. State dependence in phenology is considered at several levels of organization. The physiological effect of state variables, in terms of how they affect the endocrine system to influence timing, is poorly understood. Clarification of the relationship between state variables and timing is needed, and perhaps best addressed with experimental manipulation of individuals. State-dependence in timing is meaningful from an ultimate perspective. Optimization of breeding time is often viewed in terms of single fitness components, especially survival of offspring. State-dependence suggests that the situation is more complex. I show that fish systems are promising subjects for tests of various models of optimal breeding times.

24009: The natricine colubrid snake Rhabdophis tigrinus possesses a parasagittal series of paired glands in the neck that serve a defensive function. Early reports of the embryonic origin of the glands suggested that they arise from mesodermal tissue, rather than from ectoderm as do most other cutaneous glands in vertebrates. We examined both adult and embryonic glands using several gross anatomical, histological, and electron microscopic techniques, and our results support a mesodermal origin of the nuchal glands. Our embryonic material confirms earlier reports that the glands arise as mesenchymal condensations deep to the developing epidermis, with no evidence of the epithelial invagination that characterizes the development of most cutaneous glands. Adult specimens injected with Microfil reveal that the major network of cutaneous vessels lies superficial to the glands, further supporting a mesodermal origin. The adult glands possess a thick connective tissue capsule, and there is no evidence of epithelial organization of the interior cells.

24010: Both Neoseps reynoldsi and Eumeces egregius are lizards associated with xeric habitats of Florida. To assess phylogeographic patterns in these two species, mtDNA sequences were compared from various sites across the state. Neoseps reynoldsi occurs only on three ridges in the central highland of the Florida peninsula. Populations are highly structured, with four major lineages observed and deep genetic division among the ridges. The central haplotypes in a parsimony network are associated with the northern portion of the Lake Wales Ridge, one of the oldest habitats in peninsular Florida, suggesting an ancient radiation from this central ridge. Eumeces egregius comprises five subspecies that occur through most of Florida and into Georgia and Alabama. The major partitions in an mtDNA phylogeny for E. egregius are not concordant with subspecies designations. However, the mtDNA are consistent with the hypothesis that this species also radiated outward from an ancestral population on the Lake Wales Ridge. These findings raise conservation concerns for the loss of genetic diversity in the rapidly disappearing scrub habitats of Florida's ancient ridges.

24011: Classic descriptive and functional studies of ophidian feeding have resulted in a detailed, and supported, hypothesis for the mechanics of prey ingestion in snakes. This hypothesis, commonly known as the pterygoid walk, centers on the sequential protraction and retraction of the contralateral palato-maxillary arches. Given the phylogenetic history and cephalic structural diversity of snakes, as well as their variation in prey preference, it would seem unlikely that all snakes use the same prey ingestion mechanics. The diversity of feeding mechanics was explored through a morphological examination of the mandibular symphysis, a region generally taken to have no special function in prey ingestion. Serial sections through the symphysis of over 180 species revealed substantial variation in tissue composition and structural arrangement. Suites of characters suggest this anatomical region may perform different functional roles in different species. Observations of ophiophagous snakes reveal prey ingestion accomplished with a highly modified pterygoid walk. In these cases only unilateral displacement of the palato-maxillary arch functions in prey ingestion, with the caudal portion of the pterygoid displacing the prey posteriorly.

24012: The evolution of population- and species-level differences requires heritable variation in phenotype. However, phenotypic variation may have physiological and environmental as well as genetic causes. In an effort to elucidate the proximate causes of morphological variation in the garter snake, Thamnophis sirtalis, offspring born to 26 wild-caught females were reared in captivity. Within each litter, males and females were assigned at random to two treatment groups and received sham or testosterone-containing subcutaneous implants for a three month period starting at three months of age. Growth in head dimensions, body size, and tail length was monitored until snakes were six to 14 months old and was analyzed using repeated-measures multivariate analysis of variance. Family membership had pervasive effects on growth in all traits. These effects may be attributable to genetic variation or maternal effects arising from the common in utero environment shared by litter-mates. Sex had significant effects on growth in all traits but the magnitude of these effects was small, suggesting that differences in body size seen in adult garter snakes do not arise until later in life. Elevated testosterone levels had significant but small negative effects on growth in body size and head dimensions.

24013: Estimates of individual reproductive success are essential for determining patterns of sexual selection in snakes, yet studies which assess reproductive success using genetic markers are rare. We used microsatellite DNA markers to conduct parentage studies in two wild populations of the northern water snake, Nerodia sipedon, in Eastern Ontario. Specifically, eight microsatellite loci were isolated and used to assign paternity to 48 broods with a high probability of exclusion [P(E)=0.999], and subsequently to estimate individual male and female reproductive success. Our results indicate that 1) multiple paternity occurs in approximately 40% of the broods born in the wild, confirming findings from other studies that females accept copulations from multiple males, and 2) less than 10% of the marked males sired any offspring over the three years of this study, suggesting that there may be strong selection acting on certain male phenotypic characters that maximize male reproductive success.

24014: Northern temperate snakes have a number of life history characteristics that could lead to genetic structuring at fine geographic scales including: 1) use of communal hibernacula for over-wintering and 2) high adult inter-annual fidelity to specific hibernaculum sites. In this study we investigated this possibility by examining the distribution of variation at six microsatellite loci in one such temperate snake taxon, the black rat snake (Elaphe o. obsoleta). Sampling occurred at three hierarchical scales ranging from individual hibernacula to regional populations, mostly within the Frontenac Axis region of eastern Ontario. We detected no statistically significant pair-wise differentiation (FST and RST) between hibernacula within the same sub-populations (inter-hibernaculum distance <= 6 Km). However, isolation by distance was evident among locales within the Frontenac Axis (maximum distance of 50 Km) and among regional populations (maximum distance of 1500 Km). Conservative estimates of Ne derived from heterozygosity values ranged from approximately 600 to 2000. These values are far in excess of the number of snakes typically found in a single hibernaculum and suggest relatively large genetic neighborhoods encompassing many communal hibernacula. Our results suggest viscosity of gene flow over relatively short distances (at the scale of tens of kilometers) but substantial genetic exchange among local hibernacula.

24015: Lungs have been shown to function in reception of airborne sound in snakes and species of frogs that lack tympanic middle ears, and this lung pathway may represent the most primitive mechanism of hearing in tetrapod vertebrates. Laser vibrometric studies were extended to investigate the acoustic responsiveness of the lateral body walls and lungs of salamanders and lizards, and additional studies analyzing potential routes of sound energy transfer from the lungs to the inner ear were conducted on frogs. The body walls of several species of salamanders and lizards were found to be responsive to sound, typically showing a low frequency peak in motion (< 300 Hz) and a higher frequency peak from 800-2000 Hz depending on body size. In contrast, the body wall of lungless plethodontid salamanders showed a reduced low frequency peak in motion and completely lacked the higher frequency peak. Neurophysiological studies on fire-bellied toads (Bombina orientalis) suggest that sound energy is not transferred from the lung to the inner ear via respiratory pathways. Vibrometric experiments suggest instead that the opercularis system may be involved. Sound-induced motion of the suprascapula decreased dramatically when sound was blocked from reaching the body wall/lung. Lung-induced motion of the suprascapula may be relayed via the opercularis muscle to the operculum in the oval window of the inner ear.

24016: Gordon Walls (1940, 1942) constructed an elegant, logical story for the early origin of snakes as burrowers, based upon the anatomy of the eye. Independently, Mahendra (1938) suggested that burrowing snakes, such as Typhlops, represented the most basal snake lineages, also underscoring the hypothesis of a fossorial ancestry for snakes. This hypothesis, with some modification, has been widely accepted (Underwood, 1970; Rieppel, 1988). Recent phylogenetic research by Caldwell and Lee (1997) suggested an alternative to the fossorial ancestor hypothesis, reviving an early hypothesis for an aquatic origin of modern snakes. Can the ophthalmic characteristics so forcefully argued by Walls for a fossorial origin of snakes equally support an argument for an aquatic origin for snakes? In fact, many of these same ophthalmic characteristics are observed in aquatic taxa. The shape and relative size of the lens and the method of accommodation in modern snakes are typical of aquatic animals and suggest an aquatic ancestry for snakes. Other characteristics of the eye are less obviously attributable to an aquatic ancestor but are still consistent with this alternative hypothesis. In light of the revised historical framework, this alternative hypothesis for the ecological origin for snakes merits closer inspection.

24017: Diamondback terrapins, Malaclemys terrapin, frequently drown due to incidental capture in crab pots. Crab pots selectively capture male and young female terrapins, thereby skewing sex ratios and removing individuals with high reproductive value. We tested a by-catch reduction device (BRD) to determine its ability to reduce terrapin entrapment and the effect the BRD had on the size and number of crabs that were caught in crab pots. We tested three size BRDs, 4 cm x 10 cm, 4.5 cm x 12 cm and 5 cm x 10 cm, on both standard crab pots and modified crab pots designed to prevent terrapin mortality. We found that the 4 cm x 10 cm BRD effectively prevented turtle entry, however, eliminated crabs based on height. Neither the 5 cm x 10 cm nor the 4.5 cm x 12 cm BRDs affected crab size or the number of crabs caught, but the 4.5 cm x 12 cm BRD reduced terrapin by-catch by 82 percent, whereas the 5 cm x 10 cm BRD only reduced terrapin by-catch by 50%. We stress the importance of using BRDs to reduce terrapin captures throughout their range, thus preserving the biodiversity of wetland ecosystems and restoring or maintaining natural sex ratios of terrapin populations.

24018: The gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) is legally protected by state regulations throughout its range and federally listed as threatened in the western portion of its range. Population sizes of gopher tortoises have traditionally been calculated using standard correction factors that estimate the number of tortoises based on the number of burrows in a given area. However, correction factors may vary among seasons, habitats, and regions and there are no quantitative studies on gopher tortoises in the northeastern portion their range. We used a volunteer-based burrow count survey to mark 1174 potential tortoise burrows on the Tillman Sand Ridge Heritage Preserve in Jasper County, SC. To evaluate the effectiveness of the burrow count survey for estimating tortoise population size, we investigated 368 marked burrows using infrared burrow cameras. We observed 49 tortoises using the burrow cameras and estimated the population size to be 153 adult tortoises. Our site-specific correction of 0.183 is considerably lower than previously published correction factors and resulted in a substantially lower population estimate than those calculated from widely used correction factors. Our results emphasize the critical need to consider regional variation in the relationship between burrow number and tortoise population size when developing and using correction factors.

24019: Geochelone sulcata (Cryptodira: Testudinidae) achieves a length of 830 mm and weight of 105.5 kg, and is the largest of the world's continental tortoises. It has a range forming a 600-700 km wide belt across Africa's Sahelian region from Mauritania and Senegal in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east, and was reported still to be common in the western Sahel during the late 19th century. The information database is poor, but populations today are known to be very depleted in most of the range, due to utilization as food by local people and collection for the international live animal trade. The giant tortoise inhabits light savannah woodland, grassy during June-October rains, but sparsely vegetated and livestock-trampled during the Sahelian dry season. Refuge is sought in burrows. The species occurs in zones with mean annual rainfall 140-1098 mm. The bioclimatic range is "desertic", "sub-desertic" and barely "warm tropical - dry season of long duration", and vegetation mainly "Semi-desert grassland and shrubland: northern Sahel and Somalia-Masai", "Sahel Acacia woodland, grassland and deciduous bushland" and "undifferentiated woodland: Sudanian and Ethiopian". Using locality records, a project is being developed to map the giant tortoise's optimum habitat by means of satellite imagery. This will form the basis for recommending the creation of a natural reserve in Mali, and areas for re-stocking with captive-bred animals.

24020: We investigated populations of the Jamaican slider turtle (Trachemys terrapen), a species endemic to Jamaica. We sampled turtles at four sites - three along the southern Jamaican coast and one in northwest Jamaica. We captured turtles in a variety of habitats, including a permanently ponded wetland, farm ponds, and a stream in a karst landscape. Turtles were also found in a series of seasonal ponds where they retreat into nearby cave refugia. The refugia remain flooded, thus allowing the slider population to exist in this seasonally arid landscape. We did not observe or capture turtles during limited sampling in a large river and a brackish mangrove swamp. Individuals from the northwest population appeared morphologically distinct from turtles captured along the south coast and descriptions of T. terrapen provided in the literature. The native people harvest turtles whenever they are found incidentally. Concentrated populations, such as those in the cave refugia, are heavily exploited. We found red-eared sliders (Trachemys scripta elegans) in Jamaican pet stores and suspect they could become established in Jamaica, possibly hybridizing with the native slider. Our preliminary research suggests that T. terrapen is a highly threatened species needing conservation action in order to insure its persistence.

24021: Few studies have addressed intraspecific trends within a marine turtle species over a large area. The main objective of this study was to quantify whether loggerhead sea turtles nesting in Florida, Brazil, and Greece differ significantly in their morphology and reproductive output. Data on body size, clutch size and egg size were collected from nesting females. To place ideas in a more general perspective, morphological and reproductive data on other loggerhead populations were compiled from the literature and examined for latitudinal trends within the Atlantic and Mediterranean. Differences in morphology and reproductive output were observed among the three populations, indicating that each population experiences and responds to a unique combination of factors both at and away from the nesting beach. Both body size and egg size were significantly correlated with latitude. However, correlations were not significant when Mediterranean data were excluded, suggesting that turtles in the Mediterranean encounter environmental conditions significantly different from oceanic populations. This study highlights important differences among populations, broadens the concept of life history variation to a turtle species not confined to a single geographic location, and emphasizes the need for conserving genetic and phenotypic variation in marine turtle populations.

24022: The five-lined skink is widely distributed in eastern North America but its populations are disjunct and of conservation concern in the northern portion of its range. Canadian populations are presently considered "vulnerable". We studied effects of human disturbance on five-lined skinks at Point Pelee National Park, from 1990 to 1997. Surveys indicated low skink abundance and a lack of woody debris in areas heavily used by humans. A population decline, concurrent with high disturbance levels, occurred from 1990 to 1996. Skinks used woody debris as refuge sites and showed preferential use of large moderately decayed logs and boards having greater surface area. Human disturbance resulted in degradation and removal of debris. To test the hypothesis that skink absence in human high-use areas was caused by a lack of suitable debris, we placed artificial microhabitats in areas which previously lacked debris and skinks. Experimental boards were quickly colonized and heavily used despite high disturbance rates. Results suggested that skinks are resilient to minor disturbances such as board displacements, but not to removal or degradation of debris. Habitat restoration by moving large woody debris from open beach to the stabilized dune began in 1996 and resulted in increased skink abundance in 1997.

24023: Road mortality is becoming an increasing threat to endangered and isolated reptile populations. Reptiles killed by motorized vehicles and found on Pelee Island's roads (68 km in total) were collected and locations recorded from 1993-1996. During the three years of intense surveys, the roads were scanned approximately every two days. In 1998, sections of road that had high numbers of roadkilled blue racers (Coluber constrictor foxii) and eastern fox snakes (Elaphe gloydi) during the roadkill surveys, will be scanned intensively to determine suitable methods to mitigate the effects of vehicular mortality. The blue racer is endangered in Canada, and threatened status for the eastern fox snake is pending review. In three years 78 blue racers (11 adults/year) and greater than 100 eastern fox snakes were found dead on Pelee Island's roads. Many adult females that are killed on the roads are moving to or from shoreline oviposition sites. In the fall of each year, many hatchlings are also found dead on the roads. For example, from 1993-1996, 75 hatchling eastern fox snakes were recorded as roadkills. As a result of continuing development in the form of summer cottages, and growing tourism, vehicular traffic continues to increase on Pelee Island's roads. The future impact of increased traffic flow and continued road mortality on the blue racer and eastern fox snake remains to be seen. Our data suggest that road mortality will be a significant factor leading to the decline of both snake species on Pelee Island.

24024: Radio-telemetry studies of timber rattlesnakes (Crotalus horridus) and Louisiana pine snakes (Pituophis ruthveni) suggested that mortality associated with roads was a significant factor in the biology of these species. An analysis of timber rattlesnake records in relation to road densities supported the hypothesis that mortality associated with roads has resulted in the extirpation of this species from significant portions of the landscape. The hypothesis that existing road networks depress populations of large snake species was tested using a trapping protocol to sample snake populations up to 850 m from road corridors. Preliminary results suggest that snake populations are reduced by 50% or more up to a distance of 450 m from roads with moderate use. There was no indication that the population indices had reached an asymptote at a distance of 850 m. For some species the data suggest that larger individuals are located further from road corridors. Quantification of the road network on a landscape scale indicates that the large snake fauna of eastern Texas is subject to significant road related mortality that has the potential to reduce populations by 50% or more across a large proportion of the landscape.

24025: The copperbelly is federally listed under the Endangered Species Act as Threatened in the northern part of its range, and protected to the south by the Copperbelly Water Snake Conservation Agreement. Snakes from two populations were radio-tracked at the Sloughs Wildlife Management Area, Kentucky, and in the Patoka National Wildlife Refuge, Indiana. The movements of the snakes were monitored to elucidate patterns of home range size and habitat use, including hibernacula sites. Habitat use was seasonally compared between sexes. Home ranges and activity centers were calculated using minimum convex polygons. 24026: The copperbelly is an inhabitant of shallow wetlands in parts of the midwestern United States. 24027: From 1979-1983 we conducted radiotelemetry and mark-recapture studies on massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus catenatus) at the Squaw Creek National Wildlife Refuge in northwestern Missouri. 24028: Much of central Florida has been subjected to strip mining for phosphate. The mining process drastically alters the upland habitats available for wildlife occupancy. Thirteen species of amphibians (4) and reptiles (9) were determined to be "focal species," that is, they were under-represented at the reclaimed mine sites, relative to the unmined sites. Reasons for their under-representation include the lack of suitable substrate for burrowing species, lack of temporary ponds for amphibian reproduction, and lack of sufficient litter, ground cover, and plant structure for other species. 24029: Hubbs and Miller's research on the Great Basin emphasized changes at the level of races and subspecies; these changes apparently occurred rapidly, in hundreds to thousands of years. Miocene to Pleistocene fossils of these fishes, in contrast, suggest unexpectedly slow changes at the species level, i.e., over hundreds of thousands to nearly 10 million years, with infrequent evolution of new species. Resolution of this incongruence requires clarification of the relative frequency of short-term differentiation, species origins, and extinction. The Great Basin evidence demonstrates that fluctuating pluvial-interpluvial cycles result in rapid proliferation of new subspecies but eventual extinction of all but generalist survivors, often as relict endemics. The frequent extinctions and infrequent persistence of new species in the Great Basin seem to be the consequence of repeated loss of habitat during interpluvial stages of Pleistocene cycles. The result seems to be rapid but superficial changes in morphology without long-term change. Great Basin fish faunas exhibit low diversity and high endemism characteristic of tectonically active areas. The low diversity suggests that high extinction rates were caused by high elevations, high gradients (low habitat diversity), and climatic variability.

24030: Anchovies (genus Engraulis) inhabit temperate upwelling zones and boundary currents across the globe, including locations in Europe (E. encrasicolus), southern Africa (E. capensis), Australia (E. australis), Japan (E. japonicus), Mexico-California (E. mordax), Chile-Peru (E. ringens), and Argentina-Brazil (E. anchoita). Comparisons of mtDNA cytochrome b sequences reveal four major lineages corresponding to three New World species and a single lineage including all four Old World species. The relationships among haplotypes in the Old World anchovies demonstrate recent colonization events between Japan and Australia, and between Europe and southern Africa. A previous population in southern Africa (possibly the progenitor of the European population) may have gone extinct and been recently recolonized from Europe. A comparison of anchovies to sardines (genus Sardinops), which have a similar geographic distribution, reveals a dramatically different distribution of mtDNA lineages. These data prompt two conclusions about the biogeography of temperate marine fishes. First, a vicariance model alone is inadequate to explain the distribution of evolutionary lineages in these taxa. Both vicariance and dispersal events are strongly implicated. Second, the principle of generalized tracks, in which species with similar distributions have similar evolutionary histories, is contradicted by a comparison of phylogeographic patterns in sardines and anchovies.

24031: The plains killifish, Fundulus zebrinus, is a smallish cyprinodontid fish found throughout the western plains states, and additionally it has been introduced to the Colorado River drainage. The widespread distribution of F. zebrinus has suggested the possible influence of historical connections among these drainages. The genetic relationships among populations demonstrated a considerable degree of concordance across data sets. The geographic assemblages revealed have implications for our interpretations of the geologic history of the Great Plains. Some controversy exists as to whether there is in reality two species of Fundulus (i.e. F. kansae in the northern portion of the range). The phylogeography revealed a distinct break between northern and southern populations, suggesting that the taxonomic status of F. zebrinus might warrant closer study.

24033: Flatfishes of the family Pleuronectidae are distributed in marine waters across the entire northern hemisphere. The majority of species (49 out of 59) are found in the Pacific Ocean with only ten pleuronectid species in the Atlantic Ocean. Some species inhabit wide ranges inhabiting Pacific, Atlantic and Arctic waters, while many others have more limited distributions. An area cladogram using a recent cladistic hypothesis of relationships within Pleuronectidae allows for the interpretation of this geographic distribution. A trans-arctic dispersal appears to be a repeated pattern within taxonomic subgroups of Pleuronectidae. Associated with this extensive distribution is a wide range of life history traits. 24034: The variable platyfish, Xiphophorus variatus, has the broadest range of any species of Xiphophorus. Most work on this species has concentrated on populations in the Rio Tamesi drainage, towards the northern end of its distribution. Here, we report on the populations toward the southern end of the range, in the Rios Nautla, Solteros, Tecolutla and Cazones. These populations differ from the ones in the north by exhibiting pronounced local variation in adult male coloration patterns. One variety, termed Sangre de Cristo in the aquarium literature, is characterized by deep red coloration on the belly and throat of adult males. Another color variety is vivid yellow coloration of the gonopodium. These color variants, and others, are extremely restricted in geographic distribution. Sangre de Cristo occurs in an area no larger than ten by fifteen kilometers, with the frequency of the variant highest towards the center of the range. Yellow gonopodium is known from only a single locality. In contrast, adult male color variants in the north seem more broadly distributed. Population genetic data suggests that populations in the south may be more isolated from one another than in the north. AP-PCR (RAPD) analyses reveal less band variation in the southern populations than in the northern populations. There is also less variation at the autosomal tailspot locus in southern than in northern populations and greater tailspot variability among populations in the south. It is hypothesized that the evolution of local color variants is promoted by reduced gene flow among populations. This is of great interest because vivid adult male colors in poeciliids are generally believed to be sexually selected characters and these results suggest a potential role of small population effects in their origin.

24035: Africa has a large and diverse fish fauna which is spread across a variety of ecosystems and habitats. In fact, even basic taxonomic and distribution information is lacking for many groups and regions, complicating progress in this field. Many fishes seem distributed to the limits of their preferred habitats while others seemingly pay little heed to habitat boundaries, indicating more complex factors are in play. 24036: Lake Pontchartrain, a complex, warm-temperate, shallow basin, is one of the largest estuaries in the Gulf of Mexico region. The lake is bounded by Mississippi River deltaic plain on the west and south, incised Pleistocene terraces to the north and barrier islands and older river deltas to the east. Salinity varies from pure freshwater on the western fringe of the basin to nearly marine conditions in the eastern components of the basin. Freshwater input is primarily from rivers draining the Pleistocene terraces with occasional natural (and more recently, man-made) incursions from the Mississippi River. During the last century significant degradation of the lake has occurred due to pollution, shoreline erosion, commercial shell dredging and saltwater intrusion from navigational waterways. The fauna of the lake reflects these varied hydrological connections, with well over 120 species of fish known from the basin. However, the human impact on the lake's fauna has been considerable. In order to provide an inventory of the basin and design a monitoring program to assist with lake management, the University of New Orleans has been engaged in a four year assessment of the health of the basin. 24037: We assessed the occurrence of fishes upstream and downstream from a waterfall near the mouth of the Devils River, a tributary to the West Twin River in the Lake Michigan drainage of east-central Wisconsin. 24038: We use data from 10 visual censuses over five years of fish assemblages on small patch reefs located on the back-reef at Tague Bay, St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands. 24039: Twelve quarterly samples of the fish assemblages of San Diego Bay were taken from July 1994 to April 1997 at four stations using a variety of sampling methods (large seine, small seines, square enclosure, purse seine, beam trawl and otter trawl) designed to assess all components of the ichthyofauna. The northern anchovy was the most abundant fish species, comprising 51% of the total catch, followed by topsmelt at 22%, the slough anchovy at 13%, Pacific sardine at 3%, and shiner surfperch at about 2% of the total catch. Round stingrays constituted 22% of the total biomass taken followed by northern anchovy at 14%, spotted sand bass at about 13%, topsmelt, 10%, and slough anchovy, 6%. Marked changes in the number individuals and total biomass occurred over the course of the study. Both numerical abundance and biomass were highest in the spring and summer months due largely to heavy recruitment of juvenile surfperches and topsmelt. Very large catches of juvenile northern anchovy, Pacific sardine, round stingrays, and spotted sand bass caused the pronounced peaks in July. A similar number of fish were taken in the vegetated and non-vegetated areas, however different gears yielded varying results with respect to densities in vegetated and non-vegetated areas. 24040: Hard-bottom features of the Mississippi-Alabama outer continental shelf in the northeastern Gulf of Mexico (the Pinnacles) were surveyed to determine faunal composition and relative abundance of resident reef fishes. 24041: Populations of damselfishes (Pomacentridae) are frequently found near kelp beds and rocky areas along open coasts. They have demersal eggs and planktonic larvae. From the time of hatching through the three stages of larval development (preflexion, flexion and post flexion) many environmental factors influence development, distribution and abundance. This investigation focuses on pomacentrid early life history stages in relation to environmental factors that influence their distribution and abundance. Four locations were selected (two inshore and two offshore) off the north west coast of Catalina Island. A one meter plankton net was towed, for five minutes, in sets of five replicates per site over a duration of three lunar cycles (200 samples). 24042: A system that analyzes and displays spatially referenced data is known as a geographical information system (GIS). The use of GIS technology has facilitated understanding of complex relationships between organisms and their environment. In ichthyology, GIS could facilitate access to information associated with taxonomic collections. It could provide spatial analysis within and among species using distribution patterns of morphological and genetic characters; accurately analyze geographical distributions of morphological characters and correlate them with ecological parameters; and provide an objective measurement of the status of an ecosystem, which has generally been done based on human perception but lacked data. Taxonomic collections of voucher and type specimens and their associated environmental data are abundant sources of unexplored information. This information is highly relevant for management of natural resources because taxonomy has been built upon it. This information, when analyzed with GIS, could be used to address these areas and to provide the foundation for measuring fish biodiversity and evaluating the dynamics of spatio-temporal patterns of fish. The FDEP's FMRI is applying GIS technology to analyse the robust databases associated with its voucher collections. 24043: If Pacific salmon are a cultural icon, then their treatment in the past century is certainly inconsistent with this value. Recent reviews of their status in Canada and the Pacific northwest report about 1,000 populations extinct or at risk, and several stocks are listed or proposed for listing under the U.S. Endangered Species Act. Causes of the declines are numerous, usually attributed to someone or something else, and always debatable. The history of impacts can be broadly characterized as: an initial uninformed and rapid expansion of fisheries; then decades of rapid economic expansion in many sectors plus heightened competitive over-fishing of hatchery and wild salmonids; and finally, 20-30 years of extensive regulation, confrontation, and change. During the latter period, the issue of "borders" in management and conservation has become very evident. The Pacific Salmon Treaty between the United States and Canada (1985) provided the first comprehensive agreement on Pacific salmon and offered a means to cooperate in conservation and development. Unfortunately, it now exemplifies the problem of borders and their risk to biodiversity in Pacific salmon. This talk will address the history of salmon conflicts, the complexity of salmon issues, and describe the risks associated with the present Treaty impasse.

24044: Atlantic swordfish are a highly migratory species targeted by domestic and international fishing fleets in the North and South Atlantic Oceans. 24045: Initially, under the auspices of the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) Interstate Fisheries Management Program, and subsequently the operation of the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC), striped bass (Morone saxatilis) management of the mid-Atlantic (Virginia-Maine) stocks have showed both an initial abysmal beginning, and a final and unique result that can claim responsibility for the dramatic recovery of the heavily fished mid-Atlantic stocks. 24046: Mitochondrial DNA has proven useful for the elucidation of population structure and questions regarding the behavior of adult female marine turtles. 24047: Kemp's ridley sea turtles (Lepidochelys kempi) nested in the tens of thousands in the 1940's and were the most abundant species in the Gulf of Mexico. Intensive egg harvest and mortality at sea caused the population to plummet; by the mid-1970's, less than 1000 nests per year were counted at Rancho Nuevo, Mexico, the only known nesting beach. A United States-Mexico cooperative research and conservation program was formed in 1978 which now protects 95% of the nests laid at Rancho Nuevo. The cooperative includes the Mexican Ministry of Fisheries, U.S. National Parks Service, Fish and Wildlife Service, and National Marine Fisheries Service. Additional research support and funding comes from the Gladys Porter Zoo in Brownsville, the Texas Shrimpers Association and other groups. 24048: Hydrogeology of the highly karstic and arid Texas-Mexico border region is complex, and subterranean hydrographic relationships poorly understood, yet these aquifers are heavily exploited for municipal, industrial and agricultural uses. 24049: Fishes of the Rio Conchos and Rio Grande and their tributaries were surveyed from 1992 to 1995 and these collections were compared to historical surveys. 24050: Most often measures of biodiversity have been documented and expressed in regard to political boundaries, as opposed to ecological areas. There have been extensive programs of intentional introductions of nonindigenous species by agencies in one political area without prior consultation with adjacent political areas. When this situation involves international boundaries it can lead to greater concern. The present freshwater fish fauna of Canada could be said to result totally from fishes that have "invaded or reinvaded" Canadian waters as those waters appeared. The process continues today. 24051: The northern range limit of a species is the dynamic result of local extinction versus establishment of new populations. This, in turn, is dependent upon dispersal, habitat availability, habitat predictability, population dynamics, and metapopulation dynamics. 24053: Forty years ago, Bleakney pointed out that the factors limiting the ranges of herpetofauna had not been well studied. This is still true. Presumably, limits are set by extreme climatic conditions in some if not all cases. The northern limits are set by the severity of cold temperatures in winter or by the impact of summer temperatures on the development of the embryos. The northern limits of most Canadian reptiles are remarkably similar, especially compared to the variation observed in amphibians. Few reptiles tolerate freezing, and in those that do the ecological importance of this ability is not obvious. There is some evidence of latitudinal trends in physiological traits and patterns of growth that suggest adaptation to cooler, shorter summers in northern reptiles, but not much evidence of adaptation of pivotal temperatures of environmental sex determination, or to low incubation temperatures, nor to colder winters. I will discuss evidence suggesting that the northern distribution of reptiles is determined largely by the length and warmth of the summer.

24054: At least five species of frogs from North America survive extensive freezing of their body fluids. Their limits of tolerance emanate from the combined interactions of freeze temperature and the duration of exposure. Frogs protect their tissues from injury by accumulating massive quantities of glucose or glycerol and by relocating body water from major organs. The roles of physiological systems in the cryobiology of these frogs are varied. Some morphological characteristics and systemic functions are key elements supporting freeze tolerance. For example, the integument transmits ice crystals into body fluids preventing extensive supercooling of body fluids and the cardiovascular system actively distributes cryoprotectant from central stores in the liver to other body tissues before arresting. In contrast, the CNS and skeletal muscle function at temporarily reduced rates upon thawing that are in proportion to the intensity of the freeze episode. This then may affect important organismal activities such as the ability of frogs to find and interact with mates.

24055: Various species of terrestrially-hibernating amphibians and reptiles are freeze tolerant, enduring long-term freezing exposures with as much as 50-65% of total body water frozen as extracellular ice. Studies in my lab explore the biochemical adaptations underlying natural freeze tolerance. Recent studies have included analysis of the hormone, B-adrenergic receptor, and second messenger responses underlying cryoprotectant (glucose) production by liver and identified a novel form of insulin in wood frogs. Other studies have made the first analysis of freeze-induced gene expression in vertebrate organs. Using a cDNA library constructed from liver of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) frozen for 24 h at -2.5 degrees C, we identified the freeze-induced upregulation of genes coding for the a and S subunits of fibrinogen (a plasma clotting protein), the mitochondrial membrane ADP/ATP translocase, and a novel protein (about 90 amino acids, 10 kD) with a nuclear exporting sequence. Northern hybridization analysis showed that mRNA levels for all three proteins (fibrinogen subunits paralleled each other) had distinct organ-specific patterns and responded differently to freeze/thaw, dehydration, and anoxia stresses. Other studies have revealed that genes that are anoxia-induced in freshwater turtles are also upregulated by freezing in hatchling painted turtles.

24056: Hatchling freeze tolerance has been reported in western painted turtles (NE and various Canadian), midland painted turtles (Ontario and OH), eastern X midland painted turtles (NJ), and ornate box turtles (NE). Lack of hatchling freeze tolerance has been reported in red eared sliders (IL and LA), spiny soft-shelled turtles (NE), yellow mud turtles (NE), and snapping turtles (NE). To this list I add wood turtles and common map turtles (IN) as not freeze tolerant, and very preliminary data suggests that southern painted turtles (LA) are also freeze intolerant, while Blanding's turtles appear to be freeze tolerant. Understanding the evolution of this trait is complicated for several reasons. These include 1. disagreement over the importance of freeze tolerance vs supercooling in natural situations, 2. lack of a consistent standard for defining freeze tolerance, 3. lack of comparable interpopulational freeze tolerance data for a species with large latitudinal range and possible variation in this trait, and, 4. lack of a phylogenetic analysis of a clade with variation in this trait. More work is needed.

24057: It has long been a mystery how aquatically overwintering frogs, such as bullfrogs, survive winter hypoxia. There have been anecdotal reports that frogs bury in mud, but anoxic frogs survived less than two weeks at 4°C in the laboratory, and frogs did not bury in mud when it was available. In the field, while most of the pond bottom was severely hypoxic, the frogs were found in very cold (0-1°) and relatively well oxygenated water at the extreme edge of the pond, centimetres below ice cover. In the laboratory, frogs in a thermal gradient chose colder temperatures when the water was hypoxic (Tattersall and Boutilier; J. Exp. Biol. 200:1031-1038). Frogs have a high Q10 (around 5) below 4°C, thus metabolism is reduced in cold water at the pond edge. Finally, the metabolic rate of overwintering frogs in hypoxic water gradually decreased by 60% over several weeks, reducing fuel consumption and the amount of oxygen required in the water (Donohoe and Boutilier, J. Exp. Biol, in press). Aquatic frogs thus remain aerobic all winter by choosing a low environmental temperature to reduce metabolic rate, choosing water with the highest available oxygen, and reducing metabolic rate at a constant temperature.
24058: Several terrestrial anurans and reptiles that live at high latitudes have developed elaborate physiological and biochemical mechanisms for surviving cold winter temperatures. These animals can endure the conversion of up to 65% of their total body water into extracellular ice and then revive after freezing solid for days or weeks. Several studies have indicated an important role for reversible protein phosphorylation in the regulation of freeze-induced metabolic adaptations and documented changing patterns of activity of protein kinases A and C. New studies are examining the roles of mitogen-activated protein (MAP) kinases in signal transduction in freeze-tolerant and anoxia-tolerant frogs and turtles. Stress- and organ-specific changes have been found in the responses of the extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs), the stress-activated protein kinases (SAPKs), and p38 that indicate differential functions in cell response to stress. Other studies have monitored stress-induced changes in transcription factors by Western blotting and electrophoretic mobility shift assays; these bind to DNA at the promoter regions of their target genes and induce gene expression in response to cellular stress. The patterns of MAP kinase activation in stress-tolerant animals suggest the importance of these modules in adapting to oxygen deprivation and severe osmotic stress and identify freezing as a novel activator of MAP kinases.

24059: The 98,000-hectare Lake Songkhla wetland complex is one of Thailand's most unique and important natural resources. It is home to one of the most taxonomically diverse assemblages of aquatic snakes in the world. One species of true sea snake (Hydrophis brookii), one species of file snake (Acrochordus granulatus), and several species of Asian water snakes (Homalopsinae) live here. We trapped, marked, and released 236 rainbow water snakes (Enhydris enhydris) on 13 consecutive days in a marsh near the village of Ban Tha Hin. A total of 380 snakes were trapped in a 1.5 ha area and of these 144 were previously marked. Schumacher's estimate of the population size is 473 snakes (95% confidence limits = 406 to 567 snakes) and the Schnabel binomial estimate using the poisson approximation is 446 snakes (95% confidence limits = 371 to 561 snakes). Enhydris enhydris spends the majority of its time in the mud-root-tangle at the edge of ditches, pools and canals. Our observations indicate that most snakes are found in a one meter wide band along the aquatic edges. We estimate the linear density of Enhydris enhydris to be approximately 0.5 snakes per square meter of shoreline.

24060: We conducted a radiotelemetric study of aquatic snakes in a wetland meadow in Lake Songkhla, Thailand. Enhydris plumbea, H. buccata, and C. ruffus were relatively sedentary (mean daily movement less than 10 m) compared to the more variable and active E. enhydris (mean daily movement: 5 males = 32.6 m, 6 females = 21.3 m). 24061: Studies of the affects of natural variation in food availability may provide valuable insight regarding mechanisms that govern population dynamics and the responses of individuals to environmental change. The use of telemetry in large bodied snakes such as the timber rattlesnake allows simultaneous monitoring of multiple responses to changes in the environment. I monitored feeding rates, growth, reproductive activities, time allocation, and field metabolic rates in a sample of radiotagged timber rattlesnakes during a high and low resource year. In 1996, thirteen radiotagged timber rattlesnakes exhibited lower feeding rates than ten radiotagged snakes during 1997. Snakes exhibited significantly greater size-adjusted growth rates during 1997. During the low resource year, no reproductive activities were observed, however, under conditions of high feeding rates, fourteen independent reproductive associations were observed among 10 radiotagged snakes. Snakes in low resource conditions spent a higher proportion of available daylight time engaged in foraging, whereas, under high resource conditions, snakes spent more time in resting and reproductive activities. The simultaneous measurement of multiple responses to natural environmental variation suggests environmental dependencies in the rules of time-energy allocation. An understanding of these dependencies will allow greater accuracy in the prediction of responses of individuals and populations to changes in the environment.

24062: We explored the issue of predator specialization by examining dietary variation in the widespread North American long-nosed snake, Rhinocheilus lecontei. We examined the stomach contents of more than 800 museum specimens, and supplemented our findings with published dietary records. Sixty-six percent of 134 prey eaten by R. lecontei were lizards, 26% were mammals, and 6% were squamate eggs; teiid lizards of the genus Cnemidophorus comprised 72% of all lizard prey. Mexican R. lecontei that contained food were significantly larger than specimens from the United States and consumed a higher percentage of mammals. To assess the relative degree of trophic niche breadth of R. lecontei, we compared the frequency of lizards and of Cnemidophorus in the diet of long-nosed snakes with the frequency with which other terrestrial alethinophidian snakes consumed lizards as modal prey and with which these same serpents ate the lizard genus they most commonly fed on. Although there are no statistical reasons for labeling R. lecontei a specialist, its diet might often be restricted to lizards and even to Cnemidophorus.

24063: Predation by introduced vertebrates caused the near extinction of the giant lizard of the Canarian island of El Hierro, Gallotia simonyi (Sauria, Lacertidae). Thus, antipredator behavior such as escape (sprint performance) may have played a major role. We studied temperature dependent sprint performance in the captive population of the giant lizard and we compared performance with G. caesaris, a small-sized lizard abundant throughout El Hierro, and with G. stehlini, an abundant large sized lizard from the island of Gran Canaria. Among adults, maximum speed was significantly higher in the G. stehlini, both in absolute (m/s) and relative speed (SVL/s). G. simonyi and the smaller sympatric G. caesaris did not differ significantly in maximum speeds (m/s). Juvenile G. simonyi were slower than juvenile G. stehlini but the differences were significant only in absolute speed (m/s). Juvenile G. simonyi were significantly slower than similar sized adult G. caesaris. Adults from the captive population of G. simonyi should not be used for reintroduction because their sprint performance may have been hampered by prolonged captivity. Juveniles could be released although introduced predators should be closely monitored due to the lower sprint performance of juvenile G. simonyi compared to the similar sized adult G. caesaris which are abundant in the reintroduction area.

24064: In 1983 Anderson and colleagues proposed that radial arrays of traps (trapping webs) could be used to estimate absolute population density of trappable species, in a manner analogous to the visual/auditory circular plots widely used for estimating densities of passerine birds. We tested the validity of this approach by setting radial arrays of glueboards for lizards in forested areas of Guam and Saipan islands prior to or shortly after conducting total removal sampling for the same species in the same areas. One of two skink species sampled, Carlia fusca, is readily trapped and may be attracted to traps by previously-caught conspecifics. The abundance estimate for this species, as estimated by five trapping webs, exceeded the estimate provided by total removal in three cases and was less than the total removal estimate in two others. The 95% confidence limits overlapped the total removal estimate in one of five cases. The density of the other lizard species sampled, Emoia caeruleocauda, was grossly underestimated by three trapping webs. On days of suitable weather (e.g., sunshine for heliophils) trapping webs may provide useful, if imprecise, estimates of absolute abundance for species that are abundant, readily trapped, terrestrial, and relatively uniform in distribution.

24065: The Cuban brown anole (Anolis sagrei) was introduced into south Florida about 50 years ago, and is now arguably the most numerous terrestrial vertebrate on the peninsula. This, along with habitat alteration, coincides with the decline of the native green anole (Anolis carolinensis) in Florida. To experimentally assess the brown anole's role in the decline, I introduced brown anoles onto three dredge spoil islands occupied by greens, and used three islands with native greens as controls. Islands contained forested and non-forested habitats. Populations were monitored for four years with capture-mark-recapture techniques, and detailed microhabitat and spatial data was collected. Brown anole populations became very dense within two years. Green anole control population sizes and habitat use parameters remained stable, whereas treatment populations crashed, and the few remaining greens utilized different habitat types than their ancestors. Gut content analyses gave Pianka's dietary overlap values above 0.9, indicating food resource competition, and also showed that both species eat each other's hatchlings. The interaction was highly asymmetric, favoring brown anoles in all habitat types. However, green anoles survived in forested areas also containing patches of dense-shrubby vegetation, which may have helped their hatchlings successfully run the brown anole gauntlet.

24066: The highly arboreal gray rat snake (Elaphe obsoleta spiloides) is a significant predator upon endangered red-cockaded woodpeckers (RCWs) (Picoides borealis). Snake excluder traps were used to determine selectivity for RCW nest trees, active roost trees, inactive roost trees and within cluster and outside cluster random trees by capturing snakes attempting to climb trees. Tree cavities were assessed to determine current use status and captures on nest trees simulated depredations upon RCWs. Snakes climbed RCW nest trees on 14 occasions (10 climbs during nestling periods and 4 climbs during post-fledgling periods). Inactive roosts were climbed 16 times, each having documented use of cavities by non-RCW species. Only three climbs were made upon active roost trees and none on random trees. In addition, 22 gray rat snakes were monitored via radio telemetry to assess home range size, habitat composition, spatial distribution and individual habitat preferences throughout Noxubee National Wildlife Refuge, Noxubee and Winston counties, Mississippi, during 1997. Also, depredations upon RCW nest trees appears not to be random temporally. Snakes tend to visit RCW cluster areas only during the nesting season and seem to specifically target RCW nest trees during the nestling period. If non-lethal deterrents to gray rat snake depredation can be found for RCW nest trees, the snake could serve as a management tool to eliminate competitors and predators of RCWs through depredation of these species, while preserving RCW nestlings.

24067: The brown tree snake (BTS, Boiga irregularis) was accidentally introduced on Guam approximately 50 years ago, and has caused major ecological and economic impacts. 24068: In southwestern New Mexico's Chihuahuan Desert, Gila monsters (Heloderma suspectum) may avoid extreme environmental conditions in underground shelters. Because shelters that are suitable during cold winter months may not be so during the hot and dry summer, we investigated differences in shelter use across seasons. No differences were detected in entrance dimensions, but shelters used in the fall and winter were deeper than those of the spring and summer. Spring and winter shelters were frequently in rocky substrata, while summer shelters were more typically in better developed soils. Winter shelter entrances were strongly oriented toward the south, while those of other seasons were more variable in orientation. Slopes containing winter shelters also were strongly oriented toward the south, while those of spring and summer shelters were oriented toward the east and southeast. We explored relationships between the physical attributes of shelters and their microclimates (temperature and humidity) using miniature data loggers. Winter shelters provided warmer microclimates during the winter, while summer shelters provided more humidity during the summer, when compared to shelters from other seasons. A large proportion of winter shelters are reused, suggesting that suitable winter shelters are relatively less common than shelters suitable for use in other seasons.

24069: A field study of the relationship between female size and clutch depth in Podocnemis expansa was carried out at the Middle Caqueta River, Colombian Amazonia. 24070: Desert tortoises (Gopherus agassizii) retreat to hibernacula during winter months in the northern part of their range. 24071: Hybridization events between species and genera of emydid turtles are rarely reported. 24072: Blanding's turtles and spotted turtles are listed as Endangered by the state of Indiana.
